text.p: Just two months before its landmark share listing, German telecommunications operator Deutsche Telekom AG on Tuesday reported a 22 percent rise in first half profit on its ordinary activities.

Profits rose to 2.7 billion marks ($1.79 billion) in the first six months of 1996 from 2.2 billion marks the year before. But because of an allocation to reserves and special charges totalling 1.85 billion marks, Telekom's net profit slipped to 100 million marks from 700 million.
Group net profit, according to generally accepted accounting principles in the United States (GAAP), was 500 million marks, Telekom chief finance officer Joachim Kroeske told reporters.
Group sales totalled 29.7 billion marks, up slightly from 29.3 billion marks the year before.

This is the first time that Telekom has presented preliminary results. The report is required by the Securities and Exchange Commission in the United States for any company planning to list shares there.
Telekom's 1995 figures are adjusted to account for sales taxes that the state-owned company was not required to pay until this year.

"We have used the first half of the year to get in shape for our listing," Telekom chairman Ron Sommer told a news conference. "The positive development will accelerate in the second half of the year."

Kroeske said 1996 would be marked by the introduction of sales tax, increased competition, price cuts averaging 15 percent and growth in volumes of around 10 percent. The negative effects of new taxes would be partially offset.

He said business was traditionally more robust in the second half of the year and that the company expected profit on ordinary activities to rise to eight billion marks from around 3.8 billion marks the year before. Sales would fall, however, to around 62 billion marks from 66.1 billion.

Hoping to sway Germans still uncertain about whether to buy Telekom shares when they hit the market in November, Kroeske said the company would pay out 1.5 billion marks in dividends to shareholders this year.
In an unusual move to attract new shareholders, he said the company would announce in its investor prospectus the dividend new shareholders would receive in 1997 as well.
"In the first year after our listing, we will be able to pay a dividend that will rank among the highest in Germany," Kroske told journalists.
"The improvement in the results will accelerate beginning in 1997."

Because of uncertainty among customers after a comprehensive restructuring of telephone charges in January, sales of basic telephone services fell 11.8 percent to 22.5 billion marks in the first half of the year.
Mobile communications turnover, however, was up 17.1 percent to 1.7 billion marks.
Telekom also consolidated for the first time its holding in the Hungarian Telephone Co (Matav), which reported turover of 932 million marks in the first half of 1996.

Telekom gave rebates of more than 200 million marks in the first half for new connections to its Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN), which showed an increase of 81 percent to 3.8 million channels.

Basic telephone connections rose five percent to 42.9 million. Cable television subscribers rose six percent to 16.2 million, while analogue and digital mobile phone connections rose 33 percent to 2.4 million and paging connections totalled one million, up 43 percent. ($1=1.5127 Mark)
